newsitem.title: UK: IRA takes war to Aintree to make election issue.
newsitem.headline: IRA takes war to Aintree to make election issue.

text.p: IRA guerrillas brought their war against British rule of Northern Ireland to the nation's most cherished horse race on Sunday in the third attempt in a week to make the 28-year conflict a British election issue.

Security sources believe two bomb alerts on British motorways this week and the forced abandoning of the Grand National at Aintree fell into the pattern of previous Irish Republican Army (IRA) strategy.
This is aimed at bringing the horror of Northern Ireland's 28-year war home to the British public in an attempt to get it to put pressure on politicians to find a lasting settlement.

British politicians say Northern Ireland will remain part of Britain so long as a majority, which is currently pro-British and Protestant, want it to remain so. The IRA says the province is a colonial relic which should be ruled by Dublin.

Disruptions such as Aintree also had the benefit of causing no deaths, which risk alienating public opinion and causing a backlash in Northern Ireland, while keeping the IRA and Northern Ireland's problems at the top of newspapers and TV news shows.

The timing of the latest round of mainland attacks was clearly designed to make Northern Ireland an issue in British elections on May 1 so that whoever takes power will have to deal with the conflict as a priority, the sources said.

Britain's opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair, opinion poll favourite to win the election, condemned what he called a cynical attempt by the IRA "to introduce terror into the election campaign".
Leading spokesmen for Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, have expressed no preference for whether Prime Minister John Major's Conservative party or Labour under Blair wins the poll.
But Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams and his de facto deputy, Martin McGuinness, have both said they want a government with a strong majority to tackle slow-moving Belfast peace talks.

Both men say Major failed to seize the opportunity of a 17-month IRA ceasefire to invite Sinn Fein to talks for fear of offending Northern Ireland's pro-British Unionist parties, whose support he needed in parliament.
They believe the British government must take the lead and impose a settlement on Northern Ireland's 60 percent Protestant, pro-British majority.

McGuinness said recently a British government representative told him in secret talks in 1993 that the London government wanted to pull out of Northern Ireland within 15 years. British officials deny this was said.
"Sinn Fein/IRA thinking is based on coercion. They believe a British government can force a settlement down the throats of the Unionists," Belfast history lecturer Arthur Aughey said.

"The IRA never agreed with British and Irish thinking that the people of Northern Ireland must sort out their own future. This would mean the Protestants having a veto over a united Ireland, and the IRA could never accept it," he told Reuters.

Security sources cast doubt upon theories that the IRA was resorting to bomb warnings and hoaxes in Britain rather than its traditional gun and bomb attacks because of recent arms seizures and a spate of informers within the Catholic Irish community.

They said the IRA had enough guns, handguns, machineguns, Semtex plastic explosive, detonators and timers to keep on fighting well into the 21st century. It is also thought to have two ground-to-air Sam 7 missiles. "They've go enough to arm a batallion for ages. They're not short of the hardware," one security source said.

Last weekend the IRA attempted to ambush a British security patrol in Northern Ireland but the attack was aborted; an IRA sniper did, however, shoot a policeman in the leg a few hours after Irish police said they had found an IRA training camp.
The camp, hidden in a forest, contained an underground firing range on which new recruits could practice with the IRA's favoured AK-47 assault rifle as well as grenade launchers.
